groups.watches: A warning flag on sudden pumps. It flags a stock that is up at least 30% in the last 5 trading days on at least 3 times its usual trading volume, where usual is the middle value of the 60 trading days before.

groups.expects: Stocks with a higher reading will in fact move around more over the next 20 trading days.
groups.title: Unusually busy trading: forecasting how much a stock moves
groups.watches: Where today's trading activity sits in the stock's own recent past. Activity is the stock's price times its shares traded, logged; the reading is that figure's rank within the stock's own last 252 trading days, from 0 (the quietest) to 1 (the busiest). A higher reading means an unusually busy stock.

groups.title: A jumpiness formula: forecasting how much a stock moves
groups.watches: A fixed formula that forecasts how much a stock's price will move around. Each day it blends three parts: 90% of yesterday's forecast, 8% of that day's squared move, and 2% of the stock's long-run average restlessness (its average over the last 252 trading days). A higher reading means the formula expects a jumpier stock.

groups.expects: The lower the reading, the more SPY will move around over the next 5 trading days.
groups.title: Dealer gamma rank: forecasting how much SPY moves
groups.watches: Where the whole market's dealer gamma reading sits in its own recent past. The reading tracks how much dealers, as a group, would have to buy or sell as prices move; this entry uses its rank within the last 252 trading days. This recipe runs the other way from the others: a lower reading goes with a jumpier market.

candidate.claim: How deep a pullback is, compared with that stock's own normal pullback size, ranks what the stock does next.
candidate.maker: Our own cross-check: a new candidate ranking found by the research program
candidate.note: One study, counted once: the forecast program's own plan for a fear-day ranking prints these same two numbers for it, because fear days are part of this same study. The study record itself attaches the numbers to the pullback-depth ranking.
candidate.result: The ranking pointed the same way in both eras: its agreement with later 20-day returns scored +0.026 in the first era and +0.031 in the second (strength 4.3 both times), and +0.062 at 60 days in the second era (strength 9.8). That is a real pattern on one family of data, still an unproven candidate, not a validated edge.

held_up.claim: The 15.87 expected-move formula (the day's expected move equals the close times the fear gauge divided by 15.87) reproduces its author's own published values.
held_up.maker: Azrael Options, author of the 15.87 rule
held_up.result: It reproduces the author's own values exactly: expected moves of 73.0 and 81.5, and a weekly move of 182.2, and every filed map recomputes exactly. This grades the calculation only: it says nothing about whether trading on the move makes money.
held_up.sample: The author's published example values, plus every filed map on record
held_up.study: Our rebuild of the formula, checked against the author's own worked examples and every filed map

held_up.claim: Nine rebuilt vendor calculators give the same answers as hand-worked examples.
held_up.maker: A second, independent rebuild of several trading calculators
held_up.result: All 9 of 9 cases pass, with the sources for each case pinned by fingerprint in the results. This grades the calculators' arithmetic against worked examples, not any trading claim.
held_up.study: Hand-worked test cases for each calculator, including a positioning measure built from a hand-computed option formula, a spread payoff priced at three prices, and a confluence score

held_up.claim: TheStrat's 71-rule bar-labelling system can be rebuilt faithfully from its published rules.
held_up.maker: Our replica of the vendor's published rules
held_up.result: The replica passes 21 of 21 tests. This grades whether the labels match the published rules; whether following the system makes money is untested, and its forward record does not exist yet.
held_up.sample: 21 tests, including the vendor's own example cases
held_up.study: A working replica tested against the rule set, including the vendor's own worked examples

partly_others.claim: Buying the past year's winners, long-only time-series momentum, beats picking stocks at random.
partly_others.maker: A textbook claim, in the form a popular chart account published it
partly_others.result: Half the claim held: the strongest-decile version's return per unit of fall was 0.58 in the held-back years, which clears its bar, and it scored a strength of 3.47 in the development years. But against random picks its strength was only 0.68, below the 2.0 bar, and the sealed final test (December 2024 to August 2026) has never been opened, so the verdict stays parked, neither proven nor buried. A known data fault pushes that 0.68 down; a sensitivity check bounds the corrected figure near 2.09.
partly_others.study: A clean re-run on repaired data, after an earlier run was found to rest on faulty data

partly_others.claim: Even if the score does not rank, the board's pass-every-check gate picks better stocks.
partly_others.result: At 21 days the passed group averaged +2.41% against +0.52% for the rest (+0.61% against the S&P 500 fund, versus -1.12%). But its middle stock did worse than the fund at every horizon (-0.16%, -0.36%, -1.16%): the average is carried by a right tail of big winners, over one 6.5-month window.
partly_others.sample: 52,968 scored rows over 29 weekly dates, April 8 to October 23, 2026
partly_others.study: The same backtest, comparing the stocks that passed every check with the rest
